title: Taking Care of Things
bigQuestion: What does it mean to be someone people can count on?

story.title: The Plant Everyone Forgot
story.kicker: A little green plant sat by the window. It needed just one thing.
paragraphs: Room 4 had a plant. It sat on the windowsill in a red pot. Its leaves were shiny and green. Everyone liked it. Everyone said they would water it.
Monday came. Nobody watered it. Tuesday. Wednesday. Each kid thought someone else would do it. On Thursday the leaves were droopy. On Friday they were curling at the edges.
Jaden saw the plant and stopped. "It is thirsty," he said. He got the small cup and filled it halfway. He poured the water slowly on the soil, not the leaves. Then he put the cup back.

Ms. Ruiz wrote Jaden's name on the helper chart next to a picture of a plant. "Now it is one person's job," she said. "When it is everyone's job, it is no one's job." By Monday, the leaves stood up again.
story.think: Why did the plant go five days with no water when everyone said they would water it?

lessons.title: Hang It or Fold It
lessons.mainIdea: Clothes last longer when you hang them or fold them instead of dropping them.
reading: You take off your jacket. Where does it go? Not on the floor. Picture the hook by the door. Hang the jacket by its loop or its collar.
A shirt can be folded. Lay it flat. *Fold* one side in. Fold the other side in. Fold the bottom up. Now it is a small square. It fits in the drawer.
Clothes on the floor get stepped on. They get wrinkled and dirty. Hung and folded clothes stay clean and ready.

words.d: to bend cloth over on itself so it is flat and small

look.title: Folding a Shirt
look.text: Here are the steps to fold a shirt, but they are mixed up. Fold the bottom up. Lay the shirt flat. Fold the other side in. Fold one side in.
look.prompt: Put the four steps in order. Which step must always come first?

check.q: What is the first step in folding a shirt?
check.why: You lay the shirt flat first. Then you fold the sides and the bottom.

check.q: Where does a jacket go when you take it off?
check.why: A hook keeps the jacket clean and off the floor.

check.q: What happens to clothes left on the floor?
choices: They get stepped on and dirty
check.why: Floor clothes get wrinkled, dirty and stepped on.

lessons.title: The Laundry Basket
lessons.mainIdea: Dirty clothes go in the basket so wash day is easy.
reading: Look at the *laundry* basket in the corner. It has one job. It holds dirty clothes until wash day.
Socks go in the basket. Shirts go in the basket. Not under the bed. Not in the toy box. If it is dirty, it goes in.
On wash day, a grown-up carries the basket to the washer. If clothes are all over the room, some get missed. Then you have no clean socks.

words.d: clothes that need washing, or the job of washing them

look.title: Where Are the Socks?
look.text: Look at Rosa's room on wash day. Two socks are under the bed. One shirt is in the toy box. A sweater is on the chair. The laundry basket has only one sock in it. Dad picks up the basket and walks to the washer.
look.prompt: What will Rosa find on Monday morning? What should she have done all week?

check.q: Where do dirty socks go?
check.why: The basket holds dirty clothes so none get missed on wash day.

check.q: Why do clothes on the floor cause a problem on wash day?
choices: They get missed and stay dirty
check.why: A grown-up washes what is in the basket. Missed clothes stay dirty.

check.q: What is the laundry basket's one job?
check.why: The basket is the home for dirty clothes until wash day.

lessons.title: Food and Water for a Pet
lessons.mainIdea: A pet cannot feed itself, so its food and water are a job you do every day.
reading: Picture a dog bowl on the floor. It is empty. The dog looks at you. The dog cannot open the food bag. That is your job.
Ask a grown-up how much food. Use the scoop. Fill the bowl that much, not more. Then check the water bowl. Empty it, rinse it and fill it with fresh water.
A *pet* needs this every day. Not just when you remember. Pick a time, like after breakfast. Do it at the same time each day.

words.d: an animal that lives with a family and depends on it
a cup used to measure out the same amount each time

look.title: One Day of Pet Care
look.cite: example care plan for one family's pets
look.prompt: Which jobs happen twice a day? Why might water need to be checked more often on a hot day?

check.q: How much food do you put in the bowl?
choices: As much as the dog wants
The amount a grown-up shows you
check.why: Too much food can make a pet sick. Use the scoop and the right amount.

check.q: What do you do with the water bowl?
choices: Empty it, rinse it, fill it fresh
Leave it until it is empty
check.why: Fresh, clean water every day keeps a pet healthy.

check.q: When should you feed a pet?
choices: At the same time every day
check.why: A pet counts on you every day. A set time helps you remember.

lessons.title: Watering a Plant
lessons.mainIdea: A plant needs the right amount of water on its soil, on a regular day.
reading: Look at the plant by the window. Touch the *soil* with one finger. Is it dry? Then it needs water. Is it wet? Then wait.
Fill a small cup halfway. Pour slowly on the soil, not on the leaves. Stop when you see water come out the bottom of the pot. Too much water can hurt a plant just like too little.
Pick a day. Check it every Monday and Thursday. Write it on the chart. Then the plant never has a droopy week.

words.d: the dirt in a pot that holds a plant's roots

look.title: Two Plants, Two Problems
look.text: Look at two plants. The first has dry, crumbly soil and droopy leaves. The second sits in a saucer full of water. Its soil is soggy and its bottom leaves are yellow.
look.prompt: What does each plant need? Why is more water not always the answer?

check.q: How do you know if a plant needs water?
choices: Touch the soil to see if it is dry
Look at the color of the pot
check.why: Dry soil means water. Wet soil means wait.

check.q: Where do you pour the water?
check.why: Roots in the soil drink the water. Leaves do not.

check.q: Can too much water hurt a plant?
check.why: Too much water leaves soil soggy and can turn leaves yellow.

lessons.title: Wipe It Now
lessons.mainIdea: A spill wiped right away is a small job; a spill left alone becomes a big one.
reading: You pour milk. Some spills on the table. Do not walk away. Get a cloth or a paper towel. Wipe it now. Rinse the cloth.
A spill on the floor is slippery. Someone can fall. Tell a grown-up if it is big or if there is broken glass. Broken glass is a grown-up job.
A *spill* left alone gets sticky. It draws ants. It dries hard. Then it takes ten wipes instead of one.

words.d: liquid or food that lands where it should not be

look.title: Juice on the Floor
look.text: Look at the kitchen. A cup of juice tipped over. Juice runs across the counter and drips onto the floor. Kai looks at it and heads for the couch. His little sister is walking toward the kitchen in socks.
look.prompt: What could happen next? What should Kai do first, and what should he say?

check.q: Milk spills on the table. What do you do?
choices: Wipe it now with a cloth
check.why: A fresh spill takes one wipe. A dry spill takes many.

check.q: Why is a spill on the floor a safety problem?
check.why: Wet floors are slippery. Wipe it before someone walks there.

check.q: A glass breaks on the floor. Whose job is it?
check.why: Broken glass can cut you. Step back and tell a grown-up.

lessons.title: Books and Borrowed Things
lessons.mainIdea: Take care of borrowed things and return them on time and in good shape.
reading: You *borrow* a library book. It is not yours. It is everyone's. Turn pages by the corner. Use a bookmark, not a fold. Keep it away from juice.
A borrowed toy or game goes back to its owner. Give it back on time. Give it back the way you got it. Say, "Thank you for letting me use it."
If something breaks, tell the truth. Say, "I am sorry, it broke." People forgive a mistake. They do not forget a hidden one.

words.d: to use something that belongs to someone else and give it back
a strip of paper that holds your place in a book

look.title: The Library Book
look.text: Look at the library book on the kitchen table. It is due tomorrow. One page corner is folded down to save the place. A ring of juice sits on the cover. The book is under a plate of toast.
look.prompt: Name three things that should be different. What does the book need before it goes back?

check.q: How do you hold your place in a library book?
check.why: A bookmark saves the page without bending or hurting the book.

check.q: You borrowed a toy and it broke. What do you do?
choices: Tell the truth and say sorry
check.why: Telling the truth is how people learn they can trust you.

check.q: What do you say when you return a borrowed thing?
choices: Thank you for letting me use it
check.why: Thank you shows you know it was a gift to use it.

lessons.title: Counting on You
lessons.mainIdea: When you do what you said you would do, people can count on you.
reading: Jaden said he would water the plant. He did. Every Monday and Thursday. Nobody had to remind him. That makes Jaden someone you can *count on*.
Counting on someone means you can trust them. You say you will feed the cat. You feed the cat. You say you will put the blocks back. You do it.
It is not about being big or fast. It is about doing what you said. Small jobs, done every time. That is how trust grows.

words.d: to trust that someone will do what they said

look.title: Who Would You Pick?
look.text: Two kids want the job of feeding the class fish. Mia fed it last week but forgot two days. Theo has been the door holder all month and never missed a day. The fish needs food every single day.
look.prompt: Who would you pick and why? What could Mia do to become someone people count on?

check.q: What does it mean to count on someone?
choices: You can trust them to do what they said
check.why: Counting on someone means trusting them to follow through.

check.q: How does trust grow?
choices: By doing small jobs every time
check.why: Trust comes from doing what you said, again and again.

check.q: You said you would feed the cat. What makes you someone people count on?
choices: Asking someone else to do it
check.why: Doing what you said is what makes people trust you.

review.q: Why did the class plant go a whole week without water?
choices: Everyone thought someone else would do it
review.why: When a job is everyone's, it is no one's. One name on the chart fixes that.

review.q: Where do you pour water for a plant?
review.why: The roots in the soil drink the water.

review.q: How much food goes in the pet bowl?
choices: As much as it will eat
review.why: Use the scoop and the right amount. Too much can make a pet sick.

review.q: Juice spills on the floor. What do you do first?
review.why: A fresh spill wipes up fast, and a wet floor can make someone fall.

review.q: You broke a borrowed toy. What do you do?
choices: Tell the truth and say sorry
Give it back and say nothing
review.why: Telling the truth is how people learn to trust you.

review.q: What is the first step in folding a shirt?
review.why: Lay it flat first. Then fold the sides and the bottom.
